items.title: D'Imperio interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2014
items.q: Like Jimmy Cobb, you would think he’d be playing quarter notes, but he’s actually playing a real tight sixteenth note.

ctx.x: I find that fascinating, this idea of playing on top of the beat. How can you — I heard Louis Hayes one night at some club and I said, “he is so on top of this beat, how does this music not speed up?” Or maybe it does.

Maybe it does. Well you see I don’t know, because each guy’s got a different cymbal beat. Like Jimmy Cobb, you would think he’d be playing quarter notes, but he’s actually playing a real tight sixteenth note. But you see what I did, the way, my father, when he first showed me the beat, he said, “this is the way the beat goes,” and he had to do it with two hands. But the way I practiced it was I would go [drums]. So if you play a flam [drums] then you’re not playing it right as far as I’m concerned. So it’s got to…

their own cymbal beat. Louis Hayes, and each guy works differently, works better with certain bass players. Like Louis Hayes and Sam Jones hit it beautifully, and also Philly Joe Jones and Paul Chambers hit it beautifully. But Louis Hayes and Paul Chambers didn’t hit it as well, and Philly Joe didn’t hit it quite as well with Sam Jones. So everybody’s got their own time feel that works for them. Bass players, for me, I mean I’m very particular about bass players you know. And really, if I’m going to be able to be…
